statement: Let $R>0$ and let $f$ be [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$, with values in a complex normed space, with finite order at every point. With $C_w(z)=\frac{R^2-\bar w z}{R(z-w)}$ there is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form and zero-free on $|z|<R$, such that $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ off a discrete set.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$.
The function $f$ is [locally nonzero](c:locally-nonzero-function) at every point of the closed disk, so its order is never $\infty$.

conclusion: There is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form on the closed disk and zero-free on the open disk, with $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ outside a discrete subset of the closed disk.

formal.difference: mathlib allows any real $R$ and treats $R\le 0$ as a trivial case with an empty open disk. Otherwise the statements agree.

proofs.name: Cancel by canonical factors
proofs.slogan: Multiply f by canonical factors that cancel its zeros and poles, then pass to the normal form.
proofs.scope: The case $R>0$. For $R\le 0$ the open disk is empty: take $g$ constant equal to $f(0)$ and the product empty.

roles.why: A positive radius makes the open disk nonempty and defines every canonical factor.
Meromorphy of $f$ gives a meromorphic product and only finitely many zeros and poles.
Finite order everywhere lets orders add, so the product has order $0$ at each point of the open disk.

steps.slogan: Show that each canonical factor has one simple pole and no zero.
steps.detail: Take $|w|<R$ and $|z|\le R$. Then $|R^2-\bar w z|\ge R^2-|w|R>0$, so $C_w$ has no zero on the closed disk. Its only [pole](c:pole-of-a-function) is $z=w$, and it is simple because the numerator is nonzero there. Hence $\operatorname{ord}_w C_w=-1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_z C_w=0$ for $z\ne w$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ has only finitely many zeros and poles in the open disk.
steps.detail: Near a point $p$ the function is $(z-p)^k h(z)$ with $h$ nonzero at $p$, because its order is finite. So the points with nonzero order have no accumulation point in the closed disk. A compact disk holds only finitely many of them, so $n(w)=\operatorname{ord}_w f$ is nonzero for finitely many $w$.

steps.slogan: Multiply $f$ by the finite product of the canonical factors raised to $n(w)$.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi=\big(\prod_w C_w^{n(w)}\big)f$, a finite product. At a point $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, the factor $C_w^{n(w)}$ has order $-n(w)$ and $f$ has order $n(w)$, so $\varphi$ has order $0$. At every other point of the open disk all factors have order $0$, so the order of $\varphi$ is that of $f$, which is $0$.

steps.slogan: Replace $\varphi$ by its meromorphic normal form $g$.
steps.detail: Changing $\varphi$ on a discrete set gives a function $g$ in normal form with the same orders at every point. At a point of the open disk the order is $0$, so $g$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) there and $g(z)\ne 0$. The set where $g\ne\varphi$ is discrete.

steps.slogan: Multiply back by the inverse product to recover $f$ off a discrete set.
steps.detail: Away from the finitely many $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, $C_w^{-n(w)}C_w^{n(w)}=1$ pointwise. Hence $f=\big(\prod_w C_w^{-n(w)}\big)\varphi$ there, and $\varphi=g$ off a discrete set. The excluded points form a discrete set, which gives the stated identity.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The product of meromorphic functions is meromorphic and has a well-defined order.
concepts.c:locally-nonzero-function: A locally nonzero function has finite order, so orders add under multiplication.
concepts.c:pole-of-a-function: Each canonical factor contributes exactly one simple pole, which cancels one zero of $f$.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Order $0$ in normal form means $g$ is analytic and nonzero at the point.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) with [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) $D$, circumradius $R$ and [inradius](c:inradius) $r$. The signed distances from $D$ to the three sides sum to $R+r$. A distance is negative exactly when the open segment from $D$ to the foot lies outside the triangle.

hypotheses.text: The points $A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

conclusion: The signed distances $d_a,d_b,d_c$ from $D$ to $BC,CA,AB$ satisfy $d_a+d_b+d_c=R+r$.

proofs.name: Trigonometric identity
proofs.slogan: Write each signed distance as $R\cos$ of an angle, then compare the cosine sum with the inradius.
proofs.scope: All triangles, acute, right or obtuse. A right angle gives distance $0$, matching $\cos 90^\circ=0$.

roles.why: The triangle fixes the angles with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^\circ$, the circumcircle of radius $R$ and the incircle of radius $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that the signed distance from $D$ to $BC$ equals $R\cos\alpha$.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, so $M$ is the foot. For $\alpha<90^\circ$ the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) theorem gives $\angle BDC=2\alpha$ and $D$ on the side of $A$, so $DM=R\cos\alpha$. For $\alpha>90^\circ$ the point $D$ is across $BC$ and $DM=-R\cos\alpha$, which is the signed value. For $\alpha=90^\circ$, $D=M$.

steps.slogan: Show that the three cosines sum to $1+4\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
steps.detail: Since $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}=90^\circ-\frac{\gamma}{2}$, we get $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$, and $\cos\gamma=1-2\sin^2\frac{\gamma}{2}$ with $\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}=\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$. The sum is $1+2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big(\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}-\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\big)$, and the bracket equals $2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the inradius equals $4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
steps.detail: The incircle touches $BC$ at $X$, and the tangent lengths are $BX=r\cot\frac{\beta}{2}$ and $XC=r\cot\frac{\gamma}{2}$. So $a=r\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\big/\big(\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big)$. The law of sines gives $a=2R\sin\alpha=4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}$. Equate the two values of $a$.

steps.slogan: Add the three distances and replace the cosine sum by the inradius formula.
steps.detail: By the first step, $d_a+d_b+d_c=R(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma)$. By the second step this is $R+4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$. By the third step the last term is $r$, so the sum is $R+r$.

concepts.c:triangle: Its angles sum to $180^\circ$, which links the half-angles in the identities.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcenter is the point whose distances to the sides are summed.
concepts.c:inradius: The inradius is the second term of the sum and has a half-angle formula.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: It turns the angle at $A$ into the central angle $\angle BDC$.

source.note: Standard trigonometric proof through the half-angle formula for the inradius.

statement: Let $G$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group). Then $G$ is [simple](c:simple-group) if and only if its order is a [prime number](c:prime-number). Such a group is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group).
conclusion: $G$ is [simple](c:simple-group) exactly when $|G|$ is prime, and then $G$ is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group).

proofs.name: Cyclic generator and Lagrange
proofs.slogan: A simple abelian group is cyclic, a generator of composite or infinite order gives a proper subgroup, and Lagrange gives the converse.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The trivial group is not simple and has no prime order. An infinite group has no prime order and is shown not simple.

roles.why: Commutativity makes every subgroup [normal](c:normal-subgroup), so simplicity says that the only subgroups are $1$ and $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that every subgroup of $G$ is normal.
steps.detail: For $x\in G$ and $h$ in a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H$ we have $xhx^{-1}=h$ because $G$ is abelian. So $H$ is [normal](c:normal-subgroup). Hence $G$ is simple exactly when $G\ne 1$ and its only subgroups are $1$ and $G$.

steps.slogan: Show that a simple abelian group is generated by any element other than $1$.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be simple and $g\ne 1$. The subgroup $\langle g\rangle$ is normal and nontrivial, so $\langle g\rangle=G$. Hence $G$ is [cyclic](c:cyclic-group) with generator $g$.

steps.slogan: Show that the generator of a simple abelian group has prime order.
steps.detail: Let $n=\operatorname{ord}(g)$. If $n=1$ then $G=1$, which is not simple. If $n=\infty$ then $\langle g^2\rangle$ is a proper nontrivial subgroup. If $n=ab$ with $1<a<n$ then $\langle g^a\rangle$ has order $b$ and is proper and nontrivial. So $n=|G|$ is a [prime](c:prime-number).

steps.slogan: Show that every group of prime order is simple.
steps.detail: Let $|G|=p$ be prime and let $H\le G$. By Lagrange's theorem $|H|$ divides $p$, so $|H|=1$ or $|H|=p$. Hence $H=1$ or $H=G$, and every normal subgroup is one of these two. Also $G\ne 1$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The step on prime order shows that a simple abelian group has prime order and is cyclic by the step before it. The converse step shows that prime order gives a simple group. Together, $G$ is simple exactly when $|G|$ is prime.

concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity turns every subgroup into a normal subgroup.
concepts.c:simple-group: Simplicity says that the only normal subgroups are $1$ and $G$.
concepts.c:prime-number: A prime has no divisors besides $1$ and itself, which excludes proper subgroups.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: A simple abelian group is generated by one element, so its subgroups are easy to list.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of $\langle g\rangle$ lets simplicity force $\langle g\rangle=G$.
concepts.c:subgroup: Proper nontrivial subgroups of the cyclic group rule out composite order.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective [curve](c:algebraic-curve) over an algebraically closed field, with [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor) $K$. Let $D$ be an effective [divisor](c:divisor) that is special, that is $\ell(K-D)>0$. Then $\dim|D|\le\tfrac12\deg D$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth projective [curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g$ over an algebraically closed field.

conclusion: The complete linear system $|D|$ has dimension $\ell(D)-1\le\tfrac12\deg D$.

proofs.name: Linear systems add, then Riemann-Roch
proofs.slogan: Bound $\dim|D|+\dim|K-D|$ by $g-1$ with the sum map on linear systems, then subtract Riemann-Roch.
proofs.scope: The inequality only. The equality cases ($D=0$, $D=K$, and multiples of the hyperelliptic $g^1_2$) are not proved here.

roles.why: The curve gives finite dimensional spaces $H^0(\mathcal O(D))$, the canonical divisor with $\ell(K)=g$, and Riemann-Roch.
An effective divisor lies in its own [projective space](c:projective-space) $|D|$, which the sum map uses.
Speciality gives an effective divisor $E$ linearly equivalent to $K-D$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\dim|E+F|\ge\dim|E|+\dim|F|$ for effective divisors $E,F$.
steps.detail: Adding divisors gives a morphism $|E|\times|F|\to|E+F|$ of [projective spaces](c:projective-space). A divisor in $|E+F|$ splits into effective divisors of degrees $\deg E$ and $\deg F$ in finitely many ways, so the fibres are finite. A morphism of projective varieties with finite fibres preserves dimension, which gives the inequality.

steps.slogan: Pair $D$ with an effective divisor $E$ linearly equivalent to $K-D$.
steps.detail: Since $\ell(K-D)>0$, some effective $E$ satisfies $E\sim K-D$, so $D+E\sim K$ and $\dim|D+E|=\ell(K)-1=g-1$. The sum inequality gives $\dim|D|+\dim|E|\le g-1$, where $\dim|E|=\dim|K-D|$.

steps.slogan: Write the Riemann-Roch relation between $D$ and $K-D$.
steps.detail: Riemann-Roch says $\ell(D)-\ell(K-D)=\deg D+1-g$. Subtracting $1$ from both lengths gives $\dim|D|-\dim|K-D|=\deg D+1-g$.

steps.slogan: Add the inequality and the Riemann-Roch relation and divide by two.
steps.detail: Adding $\dim|D|+\dim|K-D|\le g-1$ and $\dim|D|-\dim|K-D|=\deg D+1-g$ cancels $\dim|K-D|$ and $g$. This leaves $2\dim|D|\le\deg D$.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: Riemann-Roch and the canonical divisor are available on a smooth projective curve.
concepts.c:divisor: The divisor $D$ and its linear system $|D|$ carry the dimension count.
concepts.c:canonical-divisor: The canonical divisor $K$ has $\ell(K)=g$ and pairs $D$ with $K-D$.
concepts.c:projective-space: A complete linear system is a projective space, and the sum map goes between such spaces.

source.note: Clifford's argument as in Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, Chapter IV, Theorem 5.4.

statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian [Cohen-Macaulay ring](c:cohen-macaulay-ring) and $I=(x_1,\dots,x_h)$ an ideal of [height](c:height) $h$. Then every [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ has height $h$. So $I$ has no embedded primes (Macaulay's unmixedness theorem).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is Noetherian and [Cohen-Macaulay](c:cohen-macaulay-ring): every localization at a prime is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring.
The ideal $I$ is generated by $h$ elements and has [height](c:height) $h$.

conclusion: Every [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ has height exactly $h$.

proofs.name: Localize and use a regular sequence
proofs.slogan: Localize at an associated prime, show that the generators form a regular sequence, and compare depth with dimension.
proofs.scope: The ring $R$ need not be local, so the proof localizes at each associated prime. The converse, that unmixedness characterizes Cohen-Macaulay rings, is not proved.

roles.why: The localization $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Cohen-Macaulay, so its parameters form a regular sequence and heights add to dimensions.
Generation by $h$ elements and height $h$ make the generators part of a system of parameters.

steps.slogan: Localize at an associated prime $\mathfrak p$ of $R/I$ to reach a local ring.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak p$ be an [associated prime](c:associated-prime) of $R/I$ and $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ with $d=\dim A=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p$. Associated primes survive localization, so $\mathfrak pA$ is associated to $A/J$ with $J=IA$, and $\operatorname{depth}A/J=0$. The ideal $J$ has $h$ generators.

steps.slogan: Show that the localized ideal $J$ still has height $h$.
steps.detail: A prime of $A$ containing $J$ is $\mathfrak qA$ with $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$ a prime of $R$ containing $I$, so its [height](c:height) is at least $h$. Krull's height theorem gives $\operatorname{ht}J\le h$ because $J$ has $h$ generators. Hence $\operatorname{ht}J=h$.

steps.slogan: Extend the $h$ generators of $J$ to a system of parameters of $A$.
steps.detail: In a Cohen-Macaulay local ring $\operatorname{ht}J+\dim A/J=d$ for a proper ideal $J$, so $\dim A/J=d-h$. Choose $y_1,\dots,y_{d-h}$ whose images are parameters of $A/J$. Then $x_1,\dots,x_h,y_1,\dots,y_{d-h}$ generate an ideal primary to the maximal ideal, with $d$ generators.

steps.slogan: Show that $x_1,\dots,x_h$ is a [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) in $A$.
steps.detail: In a Cohen-Macaulay local ring every system of parameters is a regular sequence (Matsumura, Theorem 17.4). An initial segment of a regular sequence is regular. Dividing by a regular sequence of length $h$ lowers [depth](c:depth) by $h$, so $\operatorname{depth}A/J=\operatorname{depth}A-h=d-h$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two values of the depth of $A/J$ to find $d=h$.
steps.detail: Step one gives $\operatorname{depth}A/J=0$ and the regular-sequence step gives $d-h$. So $d=h$, and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}=d=h$.

concepts.c:cohen-macaulay-ring: Cohen-Macaulay localizations make parameters regular and give $\operatorname{ht}J+\dim A/J=\dim A$.
concepts.c:height: The height $h$ equals the number of generators, which makes them parameters.
concepts.c:associated-prime: An associated prime is where the quotient has depth $0$ after localizing.
concepts.c:regular-sequence: A regular sequence lowers depth by exactly its length.
concepts.c:depth: Depth $0$ at an associated prime forces the dimension to equal $h$.

source.note: Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, Theorem 17.6, with Theorem 17.4; also Bruns and Herzog, Cohen-Macaulay Rings, Theorem 2.1.6.

statement: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $X$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space), meaning every [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter) converges, if and only if every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $X$ converges.
conclusion: Every Cauchy filter on $X$ converges if and only if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the implication from convergent Cauchy sequences to completeness, for pseudometric spaces. The converse is the first step below.

proofs.name: Sequence from a Cauchy filter
proofs.slogan: Pick a point from each of nested small sets of the Cauchy filter, then show that its limit is the limit of the filter.
proofs.scope: Both directions. A [metric space](c:metric-space) has a countable base of balls, which makes the sequence argument possible; the empty space is trivially complete.

roles.why: The metric gives diameters of sets and balls, which define Cauchy filters and control the chosen sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that a Cauchy sequence generates a Cauchy filter.
steps.detail: Let $(x_k)$ be a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence). The sets $\{x_k:k\ge n\}$ generate a filter, and they have diameters tending to $0$, so it is a [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter). If every Cauchy filter converges to $a$, then $x_k\to a$.

steps.slogan: Choose sets of small diameter inside a given Cauchy filter.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal F$ be a [Cauchy filter](c:cauchy-filter). For each $n\ge 1$ it contains a set $A_n$ with diameter below $1/n$. Replace $A_n$ by $A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n$ so the sets decrease; each is still in $\mathcal F$ and nonempty.

steps.slogan: Pick one point from each set and show that the picks form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: Choose $x_n\in A_n$. For $m\ge n$ both $x_m$ and $x_n$ lie in $A_n$, so $d(x_m,x_n)<1/n$. Hence $(x_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that the filter converges to the limit of the picked sequence.
steps.detail: By assumption $x_n\to a$. For $\varepsilon>0$ choose $n$ with $1/n<\varepsilon/2$ and $d(x_n,a)<\varepsilon/2$. Every $y\in A_n$ has $d(y,a)\le d(y,x_n)+d(x_n,a)<\varepsilon$, so the ball $B(a,\varepsilon)$ contains $A_n\in\mathcal F$. Hence $\mathcal F\to a$.

steps.slogan: Join the two implications into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The tail step shows that completeness gives convergent Cauchy sequences. The limit step shows that convergent Cauchy sequences give convergent Cauchy filters. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:metric-space: Diameters and balls of the metric make small sets and convergence precise.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness is the property that the criterion reduces to sequences.
concepts.c:cauchy-filter: A Cauchy filter has sets of arbitrarily small diameter, which gives the sequence.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Cauchy sequences are the objects whose convergence the criterion requires.

source.note: mathlib chooses nested small sets (SequentiallyComplete.setSeq), picks a point in each, and uses cauchySeq_of_controlled and le_nhds_of_seq_tendsto_nhds.

statement: Let $OABC$ be a [tetrahedron](c:tetrahedron) whose three edges $OA,OB,OC$ at $O$ are pairwise [perpendicular](c:perpendicular). Then $[ABC]^2=[ABO]^2+[ACO]^2+[BCO]^2$, where $[\,\cdot\,]$ is the [area](c:area) of a face.
conclusion: The squared [area](c:area) of the face opposite $O$ equals the sum of the squared areas of the other three faces.

proofs.name: Coordinates and cross product
proofs.slogan: Put the right-angle corner at the origin, then compare the cross product of two edges with the three right-triangle areas.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for any lengths $a,b,c>0$ of the three perpendicular edges.

roles.why: Perpendicular edges let the three edges lie on the coordinate axes.

steps.slogan: Place $O$ at the origin and the points $A,B,C$ on the three axes.
steps.detail: Choose an orthonormal frame along $OA,OB,OC$. Then $A=(a,0,0)$, $B=(0,b,0)$ and $C=(0,0,c)$ with $a,b,c>0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the areas of the three faces that contain $O$.
steps.detail: Each such face is a right triangle whose legs are two of the edges at $O$. So $[ABO]=\tfrac12 ab$, $[ACO]=\tfrac12 ac$ and $[BCO]=\tfrac12 bc$.

steps.slogan: Compute the area of the face $ABC$ with the [cross product](c:cross-product).
steps.detail: The edge vectors are $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-a,b,0)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-a,0,c)$. Their cross product is $(bc,ac,ab)$. So $[ABC]=\tfrac12\|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\|=\tfrac12\sqrt{b^2c^2+a^2c^2+a^2b^2}$.

steps.slogan: Square both sides and compare the three terms.
steps.detail: We have $[ABC]^2=\tfrac14\left(b^2c^2+a^2c^2+a^2b^2\right)=\left(\tfrac12 bc\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12 ac\right)^2+\left(\tfrac12 ab\right)^2$. By the face areas this is $[BCO]^2+[ACO]^2+[ABO]^2$.

concepts.c:tetrahedron: The corner $O$ and the opposite face $ABC$ are the parts of the tetrahedron compared.
concepts.c:perpendicular: Perpendicular edges allow the axis coordinates and right-triangle face areas.
concepts.c:area: The theorem compares squared areas of the four faces.
concepts.c:cross-product: The length of the cross product of two edges is twice the triangle's area.

source.note: Standard coordinate proof; the identity is the three-dimensional analogue of the Pythagorean theorem.

statement: Let $s$ be a finite set, let $f,g\colon s\to\mathbb R$ monovary ($g(i)<g(j)\Rightarrow f(i)\le f(j)$), and let $\sigma$ be a [permutation](c:permutation) of $s$. Then $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)=\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ if and only if $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ monovary.

hypotheses.text: The index set $s$ is finite, so the sums are finite sums.
The functions $f$ and $g$ monovary on $s$: $g(i)<g(j)$ implies $f(i)\le f(j)$.

conclusion: The [sum](c:finite-sum) $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)$ equals $\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ exactly when $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ monovary on $s$.

formal.difference: mathlib takes scalars from an ordered semiring acting on an ordered module, and a permutation of a larger index type that moves only points of $s$. This statement uses real numbers and a permutation of $s$.

proofs.name: Sandwich and swap
proofs.slogan: Sandwich the two sums by the rearrangement inequality, and show that a violating pair gains by a swap.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The empty set and one-point sets are trivial, since then every pair of functions monovary and both sums agree.

roles.why: Finite sums make the rearrangement inequality and the sum comparison meaningful.
Monovarying $f$ and $g$ give the inequality that bounds every permuted sum by the sorted sum.
The permutation $\sigma$ can be inverted, and a swap composed with it is again a permutation.

steps.slogan: Record the rearrangement inequality for $f,g$ and any permutation.
steps.detail: Since $f$ and $g$ monovary, $\sum_i f(i)g(\pi i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(i)$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $s$. This is the rearrangement inequality.

steps.slogan: Show that monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ forces equality of the two sums.
steps.detail: Apply the inequality to $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ with the permutation $\sigma^{-1}$. It gives $\sum_i f(i)g(i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)$. The first step gives the reverse inequality, so the sums are equal.

steps.slogan: Assume $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ do not monovary and pick a violating pair.
steps.detail: Then there are $x,y\in s$ with $g(\sigma x)<g(\sigma y)$ and $f(y)<f(x)$, and $x\ne y$. Let $\tau=\sigma\circ(x\;y)$, so $\tau x=\sigma y$, $\tau y=\sigma x$ and $\tau=\sigma$ elsewhere.

steps.slogan: Compute that $\tau$ gives a strictly larger sum than $\sigma$.
steps.detail: The two sums differ only at $x$ and $y$. Their difference is $f(x)g(\sigma y)+f(y)g(\sigma x)-f(x)g(\sigma x)-f(y)g(\sigma y)=(f(x)-f(y))(g(\sigma y)-g(\sigma x))>0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a violating pair makes the sum for $\sigma$ strictly smaller.
steps.detail: By the gain step and the rearrangement inequality for $\tau$, $\sum_i f(i)g(\sigma i)<\sum_i f(i)g(\tau i)\le\sum_i f(i)g(i)$. So equality of the two sums fails. This proves the forward direction by contraposition.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The backward step shows that monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$ gives equal sums. The forward step shows that equal sums give monovarying $f$ and $g\circ\sigma$. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:permutation: The permuted sum, its inverse and the swap are all permutations of $s$.
concepts.c:finite-sum: The two sums being compared are finite sums over $s$.

source.note: mathlib uses MonovaryOn.sum_smul_comp_perm_le_sum_smul twice for the backward direction, and the permutation (Equiv.swap x y).trans σ for the forward direction.
